newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says satisfied with current level of dollar.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says satisfied with current level of dollar.

text.p: German finance minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday that Germany was currently satisfied with the dollar's levels.

At a news conferenc after one-day meetings with other members of the Group of Seven (G7) most industrialised nations, Waigel said "We are satisfied with the dollar. Six months ago, we noted an incorrect development with dollar exchange rate. We wanted a stronger dollar, and that is what we have."
He declined comment on when the dollar was likely to reach its peak or whether it already had.
Asked about German fears that the euro, Europe's expected common currency, would not be sufficiently stable, Waigel said "that fear is unjustified. The euro will be just as stable as the mark."
Waigel also said it was too early to speculate that certain countries would not be able to fulfil the criteria to join the euro launch in January 1999.

"It is just the start of February. Every country has a chance to meet the criteria. Only at the start of next year, when the figures are produced, will we be able to say" who will actually be able to join, Waigel said.
Waigel noted that the topic of monetary union had not played a major role in the G7 talks.
Turning to the issue of German growth, Waigel said he saw a good chance that German economic growth this year would be between 2.25 and 2.5 percent.

Referring to forecasts of German growth at 2.25 percent this year, Waigel said "and that is significantly more than we could have hoped for six months ago." He added, "Germany has good chances of growth this year of 2.25 percent to 2.5 percent."
Waigel also said more efforts had to be made to solve structural problems in Germany, particularly on the labour market.

"Growth alone is not enough to solve labour market problems. Some more structural efforts will have to be made," Waigel said, adding that "solving such problems was not only a matter for politicians but would have to be addressed by employers and trade unions."
